question: In Selvi v State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court of India held that involuntary administration of narcoanalysis, polygraph, and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP) tests:

answers.text: Is permissible as an investigative tool but the results cannot be adduced as direct evidence in court.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The Supreme Court held that involuntary administration violates Articles 20(3) (right against self-incrimination) and 21 (right to life and personal liberty). The ruling is broader than a mere admissibility bar — involuntary administration itself is unconstitutional.

answers.text: Violates Articles 20(3) and 21 of the Constitution; results obtained involuntarily are not admissible as evidence and the tests cannot be administered without consent.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Selvi v Karnataka (2010) is the definitive ruling: involuntary administration of all three techniques — narcoanalysis, polygraph, and BEAP — violates the constitutional right against self-incrimination (Art. 20(3)) and the right to life (Art. 21). Results are inadmissible. Voluntary administration after informed consent is permitted but rarely done.

answers.text: Is admissible as corroborative evidence when no other evidence exists, at the discretion of the trial court.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no 'no other evidence' exception in Selvi. The Supreme Court's prohibition on involuntary use and the inadmissibility of results is absolute — it does not yield to evidentiary necessity.

answers.text: Is permissible only when ordered by a magistrate, in which case the results are admissible.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Magistrate orders cannot override constitutional rights. The Selvi ruling binds all courts, including magistrate courts — a magistrate order does not make involuntary narcoanalysis or polygraph results admissible.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review 'Lie Detection Technologies — Legal Framework and Limitations' and the clinical pearl. The Selvi rule is non-negotiable: involuntary administration of narcoanalysis, polygraph, and BEAP violates Arts. 20(3) and 21; results cannot be used as evidence.
Excellent. Selvi v Karnataka 2010 is an absolute rule: involuntary use is unconstitutional, results are inadmissible. Know both the constitutional articles (20(3) and 21) and the case name.
